nytimes_articles.abstract:
MONTVILLE, N.J. Last Wednesday night, when I heard about Trans World Airlines Flight 800, I could barely breathe. 

     In 1988, J. P., my 21-year-old son, was killed in an explosion on Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland. My family was forced to deal not only with the loss of our son but also with unconscionable treatment by Pan American  World Airways. From what I have heard about this latest tragedy, it seems the airlines have learned little in dealing with families after an airline disaster.

Curfews Are for Parents to Set
nytimes_articles.abstract:
One reason I was able to grow up in the South Bronx of the 1950's and 1960's  without getting into major trouble was that I lived under a curfew. The penalty  for violating the curfew was swift and severe. Although I got to plead my case -- a watch didn't work, the train was running late -- the judge was seasoned and cynical (she had heard it all before). The usual verdict: guilty. The sentence: confinement to the apartment, when I wasn't at school, for a whole week. 

     This curfew was set, of course, by my mother, who raised four sons by herself. Like my mother, I am a strong believer in curfews. But I don't believe  cities or states should impose them.

Dole's California Hurdle
nytimes_articles.abstract:
At the outset of the 1988 Presidential campaign, the Republican strategist Lee Atwater regularly pointed to California as his party's trump card. He knew George Bush could win a national election without the state's truckload of electoral votes, but recognized that for the Democrats it would be almost impossible. "They need it," he said. "So I want it." 

     Today, Lee Atwater is gone, and Bob Dole's troubles have his advisers pointing fingers and his allies heading for the tall grass. He is 27 points behind President Clinton in California, according to the latest Los Angeles Times poll.

Meadow-Sweet Ricotta of Childhood Memory Is Back
nytimes_articles.abstract:
WHEN it comes to Italian cheese, Parmesan is unquestionably the king. As for  the queen, most Americans would probably crown mozzarella. Fontina, Gorgonzola and mascarpone might be lesser royalty. But what about ricotta? With the exception of Parmesan, no cheese is more widely used in Italy. 

     Ricotta has plenty going for it. It is relatively low in fat and when well made boasts a rich, creamy, slightly sweet flavor. Italians use ricotta in everything from cheesecakes and cannoli to ravioli fillings, pasta sauces, savory tarts and gnocchi. In many households, lightly sweetened ricotta is spread on toast for breakfast or an afternoon snack. If ricotta is so versatile, why is it barely on the map in this country?

nytimes_articles.abstract:
Congress has passed legislation to create a commission to examine the rapidly expanding gambling industry, and President Clinton has said he will sign it. All this comes not a day too soon. It's too bad, in fact, that the commission wasn't in place before the casinos came to Tunica County. 

     The small cotton county in northwest Mississippi where 10 casinos have opened since 1992 offers a lot for the panel to look at. It also demonstrates why we need such a forum for debate and a clearinghouse for information as many poor communities look to gambling to generate development, growth and revenue.

nytimes_articles.abstract:
At dusk, the Whitehorse clan filed inside a tepee to spend the night chanting, drumming and eating hallucinogenic peyote. At midmorning, the Navajo Indians filed out just as the many Mormon residents of this southeastern Utah county were pulling up to the tidy brick churches that poke spires higher than any tepee poles into the horizons of San Juan County. 

     The Navajo Indians and the white, predominantly Mormon residents of this county say they pray for each other in these services and ceremonies, but that hasn't eased the cultural clash that may break this county in two.

pages.abstract: The 1996 Burundian coup d'état was a military coup d'état that took place in Burundi on 25 July 1996. In the midst of the Burundi Civil War, former president Pierre Buyoya deposed Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya. According to Amnesty International, in the weeks following the coup, more than 6,000 people were killed in the country. This was Buyoya's second successful coup, having overthrown Jean-Baptiste Bagaza in 1987.

pages.title: Pierre Buyoya
pages.abstract: Pierre Buyoya was a Burundian army officer and politician who served as the seventh president of Burundi from 1996 to 2003. Having previously served as the fifth president from 1987 to 1993, Buyoya was the second-longest-serving president in Burundian history, after Pierre Nkurunziza.

pages.title: Sylvestre Ntibantunganya
pages.abstract: Sylvestre Ntibantunganya is a Burundian politician. He was President of the National Assembly of Burundi from 23 December 1993 to 30 September 1994, and President of Burundi from 6 April 1994 to 25 July 1996.
